qs.q: Which of these does NOT happen as grapes ripen?
qs.e: Ripening brings more water into the grapes, more sugar and riper flavours, but acid moves the other way and drops. That is why an unripe grape tastes sour, while a ripe one is sweet and less acidic. Remembering this trend also helps you understand the effect of climate.

qs.q: For a rosé, when is the juice drained from the skins?
qs.e: Rosé starts out like a red: black grapes are crushed and fermentation begins with the skins. After only a few hours, though, the juice is drained off while it is still just pink. Fermentation then finishes without the skins. Draining at the end of fermentation would give a red wine instead.

qs.q: In which season does the grape vine flower?
qs.e: The vine's yearly cycle follows the seasons. In spring the clusters of flowers appear, and each flower will become a grape. During summer the grapes ripen, and they are picked towards the end of summer. In winter the vine rests, and it needs enough cold to do so.

qs.q: What is needed for alcoholic fermentation to take place?
qs.e: Without yeast, grape juice would stay juice. Yeast are microscopic organisms that feed on sugar and turn it into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Oak can be used to ferment or mature wine but is not essential, and carbon dioxide is a product of fermentation, not an ingredient.

qs.q: A label says 12% abv. What does this mean?
qs.e: Alcohol is expressed as a percentage of the volume. A wine at 10% abv is one tenth alcohol; one at 12% abv contains twelve parts alcohol in every hundred. The figure tells you nothing about sweetness, grape colour or the use of oak: it is only about alcohol.

qs.q: Where do the bubbles in sparkling wine come from?
o: Carbon dioxide from fermentation trapped in the wine
Sugar left in the wine after fermentation
Air entering through the oak barrel staves
qs.e: Yeast turn sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. In still wines the gas escapes into the air, but in sparkling wines it is kept inside the wine. When the bottle is opened, the gas is released as bubbles, as in Champagne, Cava or Prosecco.

qs.q: Which range of fruit is found in Sauvignon Blanc?
qs.e: Sauvignon Blanc's fruit aromas run from green apple through grapefruit to passion fruit, often with herbaceous notes. Black fruit is typical of reds like Cabernet Sauvignon, red fruit of Pinot Noir, while apricot and honey bring Sauternes to mind. Recognising the family of fruit is the first step towards naming the grape.

qs.q: A list says «light-bodied, high acidity, strawberry and red cherry». Which grape?
qs.e: Of the four key black grapes, Pinot Noir is the lightest and freshest: light to medium body, high acidity, low to medium tannin and red fruit. Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz are fuller, with black fruit, while Merlot has medium acidity and a medium to full body.

qs.q: Which description fits a Sancerre?
o: Dry, medium body, green apple and grass
Sweet, full body, apricot and honey
Dry, full body, pineapple and vanilla
Medium-sweet, light body, pear and flowers
qs.e: Sancerre is dry and medium-bodied, usually unoaked, with high acidity and pronounced aromas of green apple and grass. The other descriptions fit Sauternes, an oaked warm-climate Chardonnay and Prosecco, which can be dry or medium-sweet. Remember that the label names the place, not the grape.

qs.q: Which statement about Sherry is correct?
o: It is a white Spanish fortified wine, dry, medium or sweet
It is a red Portuguese fortified wine, always sweet
It is a dry Spanish sparkling wine
It is a still Spanish red with vanilla
qs.e: Sherry is a white fortified wine from Spain, made in a range of styles: it can be dry, medium or sweet. The sweet red fortified wine from Portugal is Port, the dry Spanish sparkling wine is Cava, and the Spanish red with vanilla is Rioja.

qs.q: In a sweet fortified wine, what stops the fermentation?
o: Adding distilled alcohol, which kills the yeast
Adding unfermented grape juice to the wine
Moving the wine into oak barrels
Draining the wine off the skins
qs.e: In sweet fortified wines, high-strength distilled alcohol is added before the yeast have eaten all the sugar. The yeast die, the leftover sugar makes the wine sweet and the added alcohol makes it stronger. Port and some Sherries are made this way.

qs.q: Which grape is used for white Burgundy?
qs.e: Burgundy (Bourgogne) is France's benchmark region for Chardonnay. Its whites are medium-bodied with high acidity, lemon and peach, and sometimes vanilla from oak. Chablis, from the coolest part of the region, is also Chardonnay. Sauvignon Blanc, by contrast, is the grape of Sancerre.

qs.q: Why is Cabernet Sauvignon often blended with Merlot?
o: Merlot softens the tannin and adds body
qs.e: Cabernet Sauvignon has a lot of tannin. Blending it with Merlot, which has medium tannin and acidity, gives a softer wine with more body. It works the other way round too: Cabernet gives Merlot extra tannin and acidity. Bordeaux is the most famous region for this blend.

qs.q: Which of these wines typically shows notes of toasted bread?
qs.e: Alongside apple and lemon, Champagne often shows notes of toasted bread. Prosecco is a light sparkling wine with pear and floral aromas, Sancerre has apple and grass, and Chablis has apple and lemon: none of those three is described with toasted bread notes.

qs.q: Which aromas can oak give to Chianti?
qs.e: Chianti has red fruit and dried herbs and sometimes clove aromas from oak. In Châteauneuf-du-Pape, too, oak brings cloves. Toasted bread is typical of Champagne, green bell pepper of Cabernet Sauvignon, and honey of Sauternes. So oak can leave a spicy mark even on a fresh red like Chianti.

qs.q: Which of these is an example of a high-alcohol wine?
qs.e: Châteauneuf-du-Pape, a red from the Rhône, is the classic example of a high-alcohol wine: dry and full-bodied, with strawberry and clove. At the other end, White Zinfandel is the standard low-alcohol example, while Beaujolais and Pinot Grigio are light-bodied wines.

qs.q: Which white grape is used to make Champagne?
qs.e: Of the four key white grapes, only Chardonnay goes into Champagne, where it is often blended with Pinot Noir, a black grape. The result is a sparkling wine that is usually dry, with high acidity, green apple, lemon and notes of toasted bread. The other three grapes are not used for Champagne.

qs.q: Which black grape is used to make Champagne?
qs.e: Of the four key black grapes, only Pinot Noir goes into Champagne, where it is often blended with Chardonnay. Although it is a black grape, its juice is colourless, so removing the skins straight away gives a pale base wine. Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah are not Champagne grapes.

qs.q: Which notes can oak give a red Burgundy?
qs.e: The Pinot Noir in red Burgundy is often matured in oak, which can add vanilla and smoke to the red fruit. Dried herbs and white pepper suggest Chianti and Côtes du Rhône, liquorice and black pepper suggest Shiraz, and honey and apricot suggest Sauternes.

qs.q: Which statement about Sauternes is correct?
o: It is full-bodied, with high acidity balancing the sugar
It is light-bodied, with low acidity and little sugar
It is dry and unoaked, with herbaceous notes
It is sparkling, with notes of toasted bread
qs.e: Sauternes is an example of both a sweet wine and a full-bodied wine. Its high acidity is essential because it balances the large amount of sugar. Herbaceous notes and no oak suggest Sancerre instead, while toasted bread is typical of Champagne.

qs.q: How should a sparkling wine such as Champagne be served?
qs.e: Champagne and other sparkling wines should be served well chilled, in the 6–10°C range. Cold also has a practical benefit: it reduces the pressure in the bottle and makes opening safer. To keep it cool, use an ice bucket with ice and cold water or an insulated container.

qs.q: A very high-acid white tastes too sharp. Which dish will make it seem softer?
o: A dish with an acidic touch
qs.e: Acidic food 'absorbs' some of the perceived acidity: the wine seems less acidic, sweeter and fruitier. Sweetness and umami would do the opposite, making it even more acidic. Chilli does not reduce acidity but brings out alcohol. Salt or fat can also help.

qs.q: What does the 'body' of a wine describe?
qs.e: Many factors contribute to body, so the easiest way to judge it is to ask how mouth-filling the wine is. Full-bodied wines feel dense and mouth-filling, light-bodied wines more delicate. Body is assessed on the palate, not by looking at the colour or smelling the wine.

qs.q: When opening sparkling wine, from when must your hand stay on the cork?
o: Only once the cork is out
From when it goes in the fridge
qs.e: A bottle of sparkling wine holds a lot of pressure, and even when chilled the cork can fly out and hurt someone. That is why, as soon as the wire cage is loosened, the cork must be covered by your hand and kept under control until it is fully out of the bottle.

qs.q: Which of these aromas usually comes from oak?
qs.e: When a wine is fermented or matured in oak barrels, it can pick up aromas such as vanilla, coconut, cloves, cedar and smoke. Lemon and strawberry belong to the fruit family instead, while grass falls into the 'other' family, along with flowers, earth and leather.
